d.title: RunnableBranch branches on the input of that step, not on where to go next
d.caption: `RunnableBranch` exists, so "a chain cannot branch" needs stating precisely. **It branches on the input of that step and chooses what to compute.** What it cannot do is **send execution to a different *later* step and skip the ones in between** — because the pipe operator **fixes the sequence at construction time.** The branch picks a value; it cannot pick a destination.

nodes.label: So it cannot skip later steps

d.title: Pausing a chain means five steps you write yourself
d.caption: **A chain's `invoke()` returns when it is done** — there is no suspended state. So to pause for human approval you must **end the chain, serialise whatever state you need, store it keyed by something, start a *different* chain when approval arrives, and reconstruct the state.** Five pieces of machinery, all of them yours to get right, and the thing a checkpointer and an interrupt replace with a configuration flag.

nodes.label: Start a DIFFERENT chain on approval

d.title: Three requirements, and what each costs in each model
d.caption: The table is the whole decision. A cycle is **a Python `while` loop** in a chain — which works, and puts the control flow outside the thing being traced. A state-dependent branch is **fixed at construction**. And a pause is **five pieces of machinery you write** against a checkpointer and an interrupt. **None of the chain column is impossible; all of it is yours to maintain.**

cells.text: an edge back to a node

d.title: Most RAG pipelines are chains, and a graph there is ceremony
d.caption: Module 5's baseline is retrieve → format → prompt → model → parse: **no cycle, no state-dependent branch, no pause.** A graph there is **more code, a schema to maintain, and nothing bought** — which is the rule this module rests on: **pay for the graph only when you need at least one of §04's three rows.** And it is worth re-reading 8.6's closing comparison, where four `add_edge` calls replace one expression for a sequence that had no branches in it.

nodes.label: No cycle, no branch, no pause
A graph adds a schema and edges
Pay only for one of the three

d.title: A node returns the keys it wants to change, not a state
d.caption: **That distinction organises the rest of the module.** A node returns **a dict of the keys it wants to change**, and the runtime merges it into the state according to each key's reducer. **It does not return a state object** — and 8.5 shows what goes wrong when you treat it as though it does, which is three separate mistakes all stemming from the same misreading.

nodes.label: A node receives the whole state

d.title: An undeclared key is accepted and dropped, silently
d.caption: A node returning a key the schema does not declare **does not raise.** The update is accepted, the key is dropped, and the resulting state looks exactly as it would if the node had returned `{}`. Which makes a typo in a key name **invisible**: the node ran, no error appeared, and the value it computed is simply gone — a failure shape this course has met repeatedly, and one `TypedDict` cannot catch because it is not checked at runtime.

nodes.label: TypedDict cannot catch it
nodes.sub: it is not checked at runtime

d.title: Pydantic raises where TypedDict accepts
d.caption: A Pydantic state model validates on the way in: **a wrong type and a missing key both raise `ValidationError`.** The proportionate default is **`TypedDict` for a graph whose callers you control, and Pydantic when the state crosses a boundary you do not** — an API, a queue, a persisted checkpoint from an older schema version. **The same reasoning 4.7 applied to structured output: validate where the data stops being yours.**

d.title: The schema is the only contract between nodes
d.caption: A node receives the whole state and returns a partial update, so **the schema is the only contract between nodes. There is no other channel: no arguments, no return value another node reads, no shared object.** Which is a strong property — every dependency is in one declaration — and 8.5 shows its cost: because a node receives *everything*, the schema says what is *available* rather than what each node actually uses.

nodes.label: No return value another node reads
So it is the only contract
And it says available, not used

d.title: Annotated's second argument is read by the runtime
d.caption: The signature is **`reducer(current_value, node_update) -> new_value`**, and `operator.add` on two lists is concatenation. The point worth being precise about: **the annotation is not documentation here — it is the mechanism.** `Annotated[list, operator.add]` is read by the runtime to decide how to merge that key, so a type hint is doing load-bearing work, which is unusual enough to catch people.

nodes.label: Which is unusual enough to catch people

d.title: Without a reducer, a concurrent write is an error
d.caption: Two nodes writing the same key in one superstep **raises `InvalidUpdateError: can receive only one value per step`** — it does not pick one, and it does not silently drop one. Which **reframes what a reducer is for: it is not an optimisation for accumulating history, it is what makes concurrent writes to a key possible at all.** A key that two nodes can **ever** write needs one, and the fan-in is what forces you to notice.

state: makes the write possible at all

d.title: Updates within a superstep arrive in an order you do not control
d.caption: So **a reducer whose result depends on order produces nondeterministic state.** The distinction that matters is not associativity: **`operator.add` on lists is associative and *not* commutative** — `[a] + [b]` is not `[b] + [a]` — so list concatenation at a fan-in records the **scheduling order**, not a meaningful one. Numbers, set union, max and min are all safe; "last write wins" is the worst case, because **which write is last is not a question with an answer.**

cells.text: 'last write wins' - which write is last?

d.title: Deduplicating a fan-in is a state-merge concern, so it belongs in the reducer
d.caption: Two parallel fetchers returning overlapping documents merge to a deduplicated list — **which is 7.2's multi-query union expressed as a reducer.** Putting it there means **no node has to know that a sibling might return the same document**, and that is exactly the coupling a reducer exists to remove. The alternative is a deduplication step after the fan-in, which works and puts knowledge of the fan-out's shape into a node that should not have it.

nodes.label: Neither node knows about the other
Which is what a reducer is for

d.title: Three things add_messages does that operator.add does not
d.caption: It is not a convenience alias. **It coerces dicts and strings into `Message` objects**, so a node can return a plain string. **It assigns an id to messages that lack one.** And **it replaces a message whose id matches an existing one** — which is the behaviour that makes an edit-in-place possible at all, and the one that will surprise you if you assumed append-only semantics.
cells: turns dicts and strings into Message objects
assigns an id to messages that lack one

cells.text: REPLACES a message whose id already exists - not append-only

d.title: One graph, three schemas, and the internal one is the real state
d.caption: `StateGraph(Internal, input_schema=In, output_schema=OutS)` — **the internal schema is what nodes see, and the other two are the boundary.** A caller passes `{question}` and receives `{answer}`, and never sees `raw` or `retries` at all. Which is the mechanism behind all three of §03's benefits: the narrowing is not documentation, it is what the runtime enforces at the edges of the graph.

d.title: Three things the split buys, and only one is about tidiness
d.caption: **A contract**: the caller cannot depend on an internal key because they never see it, so renaming `raw` is not a breaking change — with one schema, **every internal field is part of your public API by accident.** **A smaller checkpoint**: 9.x persists the state on *every superstep*, so an 8 KB raw response is **8 KB written per step, forever** — and note the output schema does not help here, only keeping it out of `Internal` does. **A boundary**: the leaky version returns the raw upstream response to the caller, which is how internal error details reach a client.

cells.text: renaming an internal key stops being a breaking change
8 KB in the state is 8 KB per superstep, forever
upstream error details stop reaching the client

d.title: The honest cost: three places to change, and nothing checks they agree
d.caption: **Three schemas for one graph is more code, and the keys have to be kept consistent by hand.** Promoting an internal key to public is **a change in two places, and nothing checks that the three agree** — so the failure mode is an output schema that declares a key the internal one no longer has, which is a silent empty field rather than an error. Worth paying when the graph has callers you do not control, and ceremony when it does not.

nodes.label: A mismatch is not an error
nodes.sub: it is a silent empty field

d.title: Returning the whole state doubles every reduced key
d.caption: The node copied the state, set one key, and returned the lot. **Every key with a reducer is then merged with its own current value** — so `log: ['existing']` comes back as **`['existing', 'existing']`**. Nothing raised; the state is simply wrong in a way that compounds with each node that does it. Which is the direct consequence of 8.2's rule: **return the keys you changed, because everything you return is treated as a change.**

steps.code: the whole state, one key edited

d.title: Mutating in place works, until something depends on it not working
d.caption: The node mutated the state dict directly and the result came out **as if it had returned the update** — so the mistake is invisible in a single-node test. It breaks against **checkpointing**, where the persisted value is the one the runtime merged rather than the one you mutated, and against **concurrency**, where two nodes mutating the same object in one superstep race. Which makes this the worst kind of bug: correct in development and wrong under exactly the conditions the graph exists to handle.

nodes.label: And against concurrency
nodes.sub: two nodes, one object, a race

d.title: Returning None is accepted, which is the problem rather than a relief
d.caption: A node that returns nothing produces no update and **does not raise.** Which sounds forgiving and is not: **a node that falls off the end of a branch without returning is indistinguishable from one that deliberately had nothing to say.** So return `{}` explicitly when you mean no update, and **treat a bare `return` as a smell** — it is what an unfinished branch looks like, and the runtime will not tell you which one you wrote.

nodes.label: And treat a bare return as a smell
nodes.sub: it is what a bug looks like

d.title: Coupling is invisible, because there is no way to declare what a node reads
d.caption: **There is no way to say that a node only reads two keys.** It receives everything — which means **a node can read a key it has no business reading and nothing in the signature says so**, and a node's real dependencies are discoverable **only by reading its body.** Which is the cost of 8.2's single-contract property: the schema tells you what is available to every node and nothing about which nodes actually depend on what.

nodes.label: A node receives the whole state
The signature says nothing
nodes.sub: every node has the same one

nodes.label: The cost of one shared contract

d.title: A node's name is part of the graph's public structure
d.caption: **It is what edges refer to, what a trace shows, and what `interrupt_before` takes in 9.x.** So **renaming a node changes the interrupt configuration and any persisted checkpoint's node references** — it is part of the graph's public structure rather than a local label. Which puts it alongside 8.4's internal keys as the second thing in this module that looks private and is not.

d.title: START and END are sentinels, and only one of them is required
d.caption: **Nothing executes for either** — they mark where the runtime begins and where a path terminates. And the asymmetry is worth knowing: 8.9 shows that **a graph without an edge from `START` fails to compile**, because the runtime needs to know where to begin, **and a node without a path to `END` compiles fine.** So an unreachable dead end is a construction you can build and run, and the only thing that will tell you is the drawing.

nodes.label: No edge from START: will not compile
No path to END: compiles fine
nodes.sub: a dead end you can run

nodes.label: Only the drawing will tell you

d.title: Two incoming edges, and the node runs once
d.caption: **The runtime waits for all of a node's incoming paths before running it, then runs it a single time against the merged state.** Which is the behaviour that makes 8.3's reducers necessary rather than optional — the merge happens before the node sees anything, so two branches writing the same key have already had to agree on how. And it is also why a fan-in is the construct that **forces** you to notice a missing reducer: the error arrives at the join, not at either branch.

d.title: Four add_edge calls against one expression, for a sequence with no branches
d.caption: **The honest cost is visible in that comparison**: the graph version of a linear sequence is four `add_edge` calls plus a schema, against one `|` expression. **Which is why 8.1's rule stands** — the sequence being data rather than shape buys you the ability to inspect and modify it, and on a chain with no cycle, no branch and no pause there is nothing to inspect that you did not just write.

nodes.label: Four add_edge calls plus a schema
So 8.1's rule stands
nodes.sub: pay for one of the three

d.title: The indirection buys a domain word instead of a node name
d.caption: A routing function returns a **key**, and the path map turns that key into a node. **The indirection looks redundant when the key and the node name are the same string**, and what it buys is that the router can return a **domain word** — `needs_review`, `escalate`, `retry` — rather than a node name. **That keeps the routing decision independent of the graph's topology**, so the function is testable on its own and a rename does not reach into it.

nodes.label: A domain word, not a node name
And a rename does not reach it

d.title: compile() cannot check the map, because the return values are not knowable statically
d.caption: **`compile()` succeeds.** The map is not checked against the function, **because the function's return values are not knowable statically** — it is arbitrary Python. So a missing map entry is **a runtime error on the branch that returns the unmapped key**, which means **a rarely-taken branch can be wrong for months.** Which is the argument for testing the routing function directly: it is a pure function of state, and testing it needs no graph at all.

d.title: Omitting the map works, and moves a rename into the router
d.caption: Return node names directly and the map can be left out — it works, and **renaming a node now means editing the router.** The map is **the seam between a routing decision and the graph's topology**, and it earns its verbosity **as soon as more than one edge routes on the same decision**, or as soon as the routing logic is worth testing independently of the graph. Below that, omitting it is a reasonable call rather than a shortcut.

nodes.label: A rename now edits the router
Worth it at two edges on one decision
nodes.sub: or when the logic needs testing

d.title: A router can return END, or a list
d.caption: Two capabilities that are easy to miss. **Returning `END` terminates from a conditional edge**, so a router can decide the run is finished rather than routing to a node that does nothing. And **returning a list fans out to several nodes** — `['small', 'large']` runs both — which makes a conditional edge a dynamic fan-out rather than only a choice, with 8.3's reducers then required on anything they both write.

d.title: Command returns the update and the destination together
d.caption: A node returning a `Command` carries **both the state update and where to go next in one return statement** — where the conditional-edge version needs a state write plus a router that reads it. Which is a real simplification for the handoff case in §03, and §04 is the price: **the destination now lives inside a node body, so the drawn graph cannot show it.**

nodes.label: The alternative: a write plus a router
And the drawing can no longer see it

d.title: The handoff is one return statement, which is what makes the trace readable
d.caption: A triage node decides it is the wrong agent and **transfers control, carrying a reason**. This is what module 12's multi-agent work is built on — and **the handoff being one return statement, rather than a state write plus a router that reads it, is what makes a trace of a multi-agent run readable**, because the transfer and its justification appear together in one place rather than split across two nodes and a key.

d.title: The drawn graph becomes incomplete, and the annotation is not enforced
d.caption: **With conditional edges you can draw the graph and see every path. With `Command` the destinations live inside node bodies, so the drawn graph is incomplete** — the renderer has no way to know where a node might send execution. The `Command[Literal[...]]` annotation restores it, **it is optional, and skipping it costs you the only diagram anyone looks at.** Which makes it one of those annotations worth treating as **mandatory by convention**: not enforced, cheap, and what it protects is legibility for someone who is not you.

d.title: The default limit is tuned for not interrupting legitimate work
d.caption: An unbounded cycle ran **10,007 supersteps** before `GraphRecursionError` — and the limit this version reports is the same 10,007, so the default is **high enough that a bug burns ten thousand steps before anything stops it.** Setting it explicitly is one line of config, and **for any graph with a cycle, setting it deliberately and low is the cheap protection** — because the default is tuned for not interrupting legitimate work rather than for catching your bug quickly.

d.title: Two stream modes for two different questions
d.caption: **`updates` is the debugging view**: it shows exactly what each node contributed, **keyed by node name** — which is what you want when a key has the wrong value and you need to know which node put it there. **`values` is the progress view**, useful for showing a user how far along a run is — and note the off-by-one: **it emits the input state before any node has run**, so the first event is not a result.

cells.text: each node's contribution, keyed by name
the whole state after each step
progress - and it emits the input first

d.title: The graph can draw itself, which is the cheapest review artefact available
d.caption: `get_graph().draw_ascii()` prints the topology with no dependencies and nothing to configure — `__start__`, then each node, then the edges. **Worth running on every graph you write**, because it is the only artefact that catches 8.6's dead end (a node with no path to `END` compiles fine) and it is the thing 8.8 warned `Command` makes incomplete. **One line, and it is the only diagram anyone looks at.**

nodes.label: Run it on every graph
nodes.sub: it is the only diagram anyone reads
